why: B opens on concrete, plain-word questions (do they want this, should we, can we) and is more actionable; A leans on a famous-name framework recitation (Cagan, 2017) in bullets and says 'three risks remain' while listing four.
B adds a clause that gives real information and keeps the student in control ('you shape the rules together'), while A's 'You are not drafting from a blank page' is a low-value restatement.
The slide title and the named point sit together at the close, and the author's taste is for naming the generalisation. A makes the title carry the point, so the closing line loses its place.
'Exercise' names what the student does; 'prompts' is narrower and less accurate for a comparison across sessions.
Shorter; 'The move is the same every time' is a low-value orientation/restatement sentence that adds nothing.
Matches the author's kept call: short core-of-next-phase line; A was too long and in the wrong frame.
The count in the title does no memory work, and the author turns counts into plain frames. B is also shorter.
A names the concrete thing students will see, MCP-connector tools landing in the same set. B's 'what it leaves out' is vague.
B's added 'This is your side-quest lane' is a low-value orienting sentence; shorter wins and 'side-quest' is an invented term.
A puts the student in control ('You, in a way, compel') and matches the author's kept wording; B is the passive 'You get'.
Matches the author's kept wording: compact and gives the recommended /statusline option, with the oldskool label.
Author's reason: 'Everything built in these four sittings is on your side' is wasted words. A's 'All of it on your side.' is the kept version.
The added line is a short, low-value closer that restates the point already made; shorter wins.
The author kept 'You are testing, and you are learning.' because the duplication tells students this is an experiment and gives the why.
Opens on what the student does, concrete and short; B is wordy, abstract ('press a plan harder than you need to consume'), and a passive claim.
Fewer words: cuts the 'main lane' restatement and the sentence that repeats the worktree mechanism, keeping the one useful pointer.
B adds a kicker ('doesn't have to be in your head to be in your hands') and a clever put-down line ('Curating it would be theatre'); A is shorter and neutral.
Same text; B drops the bold lead-ins, which are visual noise on a story slide and read faster and more neutral.
A bolds only the defined term, as the author does in AE101 ('An **eval** is…'). B bolds three whole sentences, which adds visual noise and weakens the emphasis on the term being taught.
